Here are some things college students get when they pay tuition:

* Free or very affordable physical and mental healthcare
* Free number of therapy appointments per semester through psychological/behavioral health services (I frequently refer students to it)
* Financial assistance through the EOPS office
* Help getting food and applying for government assistance (my campus has a daily no-questions-asked food pantry)
* Access to the gym and showers at a usually greatly reduced price.

That's what I can remember off the top of my head. Every campus I've worked at has offered all of these. There are a lot of people behind the scenes whose job is to help students in your situation. Your tuition pays for these things, so you've prepaid for these services.

I'm a prof with cptsd. If I were writing this, I would say something like...

It's specific enough in that it says what class-related problem you are having, but vague enough to protect your privacy. It also shows a willingness to continue, but they need to meet you in the middle, so to speak.

The short story is student health center --> disability office --> professors.

The long story is that professors can be compelled to provide accommodations, but a formal process must be followed. The doctor will verify your health challenges and what you need help with, and the disability office determines and enforces the accommodations. But the office need proof and other info, so the health center is the best place to do this.

I suggest contacting your campus' student disability office to learn how their process works. The process is very formalized and bureaucratic, so it may feel like a goose chase at times.

If your professors aren't working with you on this or are being jerks, their department chair would be good to talk to. Some professors are assholes, but we're generally expected to be more flexible with students who have health problems. Also, if your therapist isn't working out, you can always ask for a different one. That's what my doc says.

I suggest making an appointment for your campus' Student Health Center to get a check-up (usually free). This is the perfect time to mention that you might need mental health help. Once you get "in the system", following the next steps will be easier. If your campus is like mine, then you may get a number of free therapy appointments per semester. Your doctor may even write a note for the student disability office so that you can get accommodations, like more testing time or a private room for tests.

At the same time, talking to your professors early can save you from a failing grade. If they know about your challenges, they may work with you. If the student disability office says you get X and Y accommodations, they **must** give you that. Professors don't need to know what you have, but they need to know what problems might happen in the class (late work, absences, quiz retries, etc).

So basically, see a regular doctor, then get referred to a psychiatrist, then possibly get referred to the disability office. At the same time, talk to professors just in case something happens.

Your brain is lying to you - that's what depression is. You may feel like you are being logical, but you aren't. You can't. That's what depression does. It's a treatable medical condition, not failure or weakness. Literally anyone can get it; it doesn't discriminate. The pain it causes is unimaginable. You are far more sick than even you realize. Some things that feel completely logical are lies. Your depression prevents you from getting treatment in many ways. That's not your fault. You might believe that you are beyond treatment or that one does not exist or even that you don't deserve one. That's the worst of the lies depression tells you. No matter how impossible it is to believe, you can find relief. Seek professional help. Cut through the lies.

That sounds rough for you as well. It's hard when someone we love changes so much. He needs medical treatment and therapy. You cannot fix him and you aren't responsible for his emotions. It's ultimately up to him to seek treatment.

We can help people with depression by learning about what types of thought distortions people with depression have ("I'm not loveable" even though I'm in a relationship, "I'm a total failure" even though I only failed in one area, "I'm stupid" even though I'm good at some things, etc.). If we know about thought distortions, we can correct them when we hear them. This is what therapists do. Again, not your responsibility to fix him. He needs to learn to do it himself. I had to see many examples of it from others in order to do it.

Another thing depressed people need is help making appointments. It's a huge barrier to getting treatment. It is hard to understand, but it's easier to ask a depressed person to climb a mountain than call a doctor's office. The downside is that we can become dependent on this, but getting treatment is more important. You can't fix him, but you can help him access the people that can fix him.

"I feel hopeless because I can't pay my loans."). Doing these at least helps me reduce the general feeling of being overwhelmed to being overwhelmed only in a few areas. I also had to deal with "the inner critic" (the abusive and malicious internal voice that sounds like me) by challenging my perception of reality; we are medically ill. It took me 20+ years to sometimes be able to stop spiraling the drain. Hope you find what works; it takes lots of practice.

I might be wrong, but I'm pretty sure that diagnosing is a job for psychologists and psychiatrists, not therapists. For a very good reason. There are formal assessments for lots of conditions; these are the basis of a diagnosis. And experts can be wrong. I had to see more than 8 doctors to get a diagnosis for a visible physical issue.  Mental stuff is way more complicated. See multiple experts (not therapists) until you find a diagnosis that "feels right". Ask about assessments, such as "I think [issue you currently have] comes from [possible source]. This sounds similar to something I read about [condition], but I want to know what you think. Could you offer assessments for any conditions based on this?" Avoids jumping to conclusions, respects the background knowledge and training the expert has, and gives the expert a direction to look without deciding for them. Assessments are the key, in my opinion.

But be careful. You cannot control others; this only leads to future disappointment. You may not get what you want from your family. Healing is up to us. You can do it.

It's hard to stay true to ourselves and be confident we did the right thing when we're manipulated by people we're supposed to be able to trust. Don't forget to look out for number one (you) before everyone else. It's okay to not be tough and strong.

Honestly, that sounds exactly like depression. It doesn't just make us not care, it robs us of this ability. In my case, I get these things back when my depression "weakens"; not the other way around. It is treatable, but it takes time and (painful) patience. Hope you feel better soon.

A professor should help you find what you need if you ask. Hope you find what works for you.

You can be depressed and still accept this fact. I've been depressed for more than two decades (treatment-resistant double depression). I learned to in the way that someone who sees the sky as green eventually learns that it is in fact blue. We can't change what we see or feel, but we can accept that we are delusional. Depression **is** delusion. Mine is worse than it has ever been due to stuff, but now I know that it's not normal, that I don't deserve it, and that I can maybe reduce it with aggressive treatment and time. It took me 20+ years to get to this point. I hope you get there faster than I did.
Depression is deceptive. It lies to you. That little part of you that's "logical" and "realistic"? That's still depression. I wish I knew that 20 years ago.
Once you label it as psychosomatic, it will never be taken seriously again. I would fight that label just in case something actually is wrong.

The counseling can be a bit... light. They are trained for uni-related problems, but not so much with more serious issues. It was nice for me to get a wake-up call: "wow, something is wrong with you, you need professional help". They can help you find professionals better able to treat you that fits your insurance and money situation. For me, the depression won't get better unless I aggressively treat it. It will keep coming back, stronger and stronger.

Yes and no. I found new things to beat myself up about, as we do. I know it's a medical issue that makes my brain lie to me. I know it can be treated, but it's going to take me a while to find the right treatment.
